Robot mechanisms · a field gauge

What Holds the Direction You Want to Move?

Forty robot mechanisms read as constraint devices, from the revolute pair to the jamming gripper, with a computational lab that measures what is actually in the load path.

01 — QUESTION

The question

Pick up a screwdriver and hold it still in the air. Six things could happen to it and are not happening: it could slide in three directions and turn about three axes. Your arm is preventing all six. Now ask which part of you is doing the preventing in each case, and you have asked the only question about robot mechanisms that does not have an obvious answer.

A mechanism is usually introduced as a device that produces motion. It is more useful to introduce it as a device that removes it. A free rigid body in space has six degrees of freedom. Every joint you add to a chain takes some away and hands a smaller number back; every closed loop you build takes more away again. What arrives at the tool is the residue.1, 2 The freedoms that survive are what the machine can do. The constraints that were imposed are what the machine can carry. Those are not two topics. They are the same ledger read in two directions, and a mechanism is the bargain struck between them.

The bargain is easy to state and hard to see, because the interesting part is invisible in a drawing. A drawing shows you where the links are. It does not show you, for any particular direction you might push the tool in, what actually stops it from moving that way. Sometimes the answer is a lump of steel. Sometimes it is a gearbox that will yield a fraction of a degree under load and give it back when you let go. Sometimes it is a servo loop, and the answer changes when someone hits the emergency stop. These three are not variations on a theme. They fail differently, they age differently, they cost differently, and they are the reason two machines with identical kinematic diagrams behave nothing alike.

What holds the direction you want to move?

That is the question this article is organised around, and it is chosen because it is awkward. The directions a machine holds are usually held well; it is a structural problem and structures are cheap. The directions a machine moves have to be held by whatever is producing the motion, and that is an actuator, and actuators are soft. So for any mechanism there is a set of directions that are strong and useless and a set that are weak and load- bearing, and the whole history of robot architecture is attempts to shrink that gap without giving up the motion.

Forty mechanisms are catalogued here on a common gauge, from a single revolute pair to a granular jamming gripper, and a computational lab of ten experiments produces every figure quoted. The finding is not the one the question implies. The question assumes the answer varies interestingly across architectures. It does not: across the nineteen complete machines in the census, 17 of them — 89.5 per cent — bottom out on exactly the same thing, a transmission. What varies by a factor of 56 is not what is holding the direction but how many things are standing in the load path between the tool and that transmission, and whether they are stacked end to end or working side by side. The right question turned out to be the one underneath it.

02 — READING

How to read a plate

The standard treatments set this out as kinematics: frames, Jacobians, inverse solutions.3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 The gauge below is not a rival to any of that. It is a bookkeeping device for one question those treatments answer only in passing, and it is deliberately coarse.

Each catalogued mechanism gets a plate with four fields and a gauge. The four fields are always the same: what the mechanism delivers, what it is held by, where its weakest hold is, and when it gives way. The gauge is a hold card.

A hold card has six lanes, one for each freedom of the output body in its own frame: three translations and three rotations. Each lane is drawn as a load path running from the tool at the top down to the frame at the bottom, and the symbol in the middle of the lane says what carries the load on the way down. An amber lane is a direction the mechanism can move the tool in. A plain lane is one it is supposed to hold still.

The symbols come from a ladder of six rungs. The ladder orders kinds of support, from nothing at all to the floor.

the support ladder

S0nothing. The direction is free. A passive joint nobody is driving, a soft body nobody is pressurising. S1a control loop. Held by a servo, to whatever stiffness the loop has. Disappears entirely when the power does. S2a transmission. Held through a gear train, a screw or a fluid column. Survives a power cut only if it is self-locking or braked. S3a member in bending. Structural, and the softest structural case: a cantilever deflects as the cube of its length. S4a member in tension or compression. Structural, loaded along its own axis, where material is stiffest. S5a bearing or guideway into the frame. The load reaches ground without deflecting a link on the way.

Two rules govern the ladder and both matter. First, a lane's rung is set by the weakest element in its load path, so a bearing behind a gearbox is still a gearbox. Second — and this is a real limitation, not a disclaimer — the ladder records what kind of thing is holding a direction, and says nothing whatever about how stiff that thing is. Two lanes can sit on the same rung and differ by four orders of magnitude in newtons per metre. That limitation does work later: it is exactly why a SCARA's famous selective compliance does not show up on its card, and exactly why a soft continuum arm and a steel flexure land on the same rung.

Three numbers are carried on every card. D is the lowest rung among the lanes the mechanism moves: how well the machine holds the directions it is for. H is the lowest rung among the lanes it holds: how well it resists what it is not for. nu is the number of compliant elements in series in the weakest moved direction's path, divided by the number of independent paths sharing that direction. It is the factor by which the architecture multiplies one element's compliance before the tool feels it, and it turns out to be the discriminating quantity.

Where a mechanism's moved lanes outnumber its mobility, the card is recording coupling: the tool can be pushed in more directions than the machine has independent commands, because some of those directions are locked to each other. Five of the forty plates are in that condition, and it is always deliberate.

03 — PAIRS

The lower pairs

Reuleaux's distinction between lower and higher pairs is the oldest useful idea in the subject and it is a distinction about contact.1 A lower pair touches over a surface; a higher pair touches along a line or at a point. There are exactly six lower pairs, and the reason there are six rather than some other number is a fact about the group of rigid-body displacements: they correspond to the six one- and two- and three-dimensional subgroups that a surface-to-surface contact can generate.9, 10

Every one of the six is a device for keeping five, four or three directions and giving the rest away. What the hold cards show, and what a freedom count alone does not, is that the six are not equally good at the keeping.

The revolute pair, and why it is the good one

A revolute pair gives away one rotation and holds the other five directions through rolling elements running on races that are carried directly by the housing. Nothing bends on the way to the frame. It is the only lower pair whose entire held set sits on the top rung, and that single fact explains why robot arms are built almost entirely out of them. The load path from the tool to the floor of a six-axis arm passes through six revolute joints and, in the held directions, never once passes through anything that flexes.

The prismatic pair, and why it is not

A prismatic pair also gives away exactly one freedom. On a mobility count the two are interchangeable, and a great deal of confusion follows from that.11 They are not interchangeable. A linear guide carries forces across its rails into the frame perfectly well, but it carries moments over the short contact length of a bearing block, in bending. The moment rating, not the load rating, is the number that sizes every linear axis in practice, and it is two rungs below the revolute's worst case. Every architecture built from prismatic pairs inherits this, and the inheritance is visible three sections further on.

The screw, and the only joint that holds its own freedom

Two of the six pairs are peculiar. The helical pair couples a translation and a rotation in a fixed ratio, so it has one freedom but moves two lanes on its card; and because the load in that coupled direction has to turn the helix to make any progress, the pair can hold its own moved direction without power. It is the only lower pair that can. Section seven is about the price.

The other peculiarity is not a lower pair at all. A flexure hinge has no rubbing surface anywhere: it is a thinned section of one continuous piece of material, and its rotation is elastic rather than kinematic.12, 13 That makes it the only element in the whole census whose moved direction is held by structure rather than by an actuator, which is why precision mechanisms use flexures wherever the range allows and why nobody builds a robot arm out of them.14, 15, 16, 17

The systematic account of which combinations of pairs produce which motion patterns is Phillips's, and it is worth knowing that the enumeration is finished rather than open: the freedoms available to a mechanism designer are a closed list, and the design work is in choosing among them rather than in finding new ones.18, 19

Unilateral elements

Three plates in this family carry a hatched mark meaning the constraint works in one direction only. A higher pair holds along its contact normal and only in compression; a cable holds in tension and holds nothing at all in compression; a ball leaves its socket beyond a cone angle. Unilaterality is not a minor caveat. It changes the arithmetic of the whole machine: n freedoms constrained by unilateral elements need n+1 of them, and the surplus is what a cable robot spends most of its design effort on.20, 21

04 — COUNTING

Counting what is left

Given a set of links and joints, how many freedoms survive? The standard answer has been in circulation for a century in several equivalent forms and is usually credited to Chebychev, Grübler and Kutzbach:22, 23

M = λ(n − j − 1) + Σ fi

with n the number of links counting ground, j the number of joints, fi each joint's freedom, and λ the dimension of the space the mechanism works in — six for spatial, three for planar. The formula has an honest derivation: start with 6(n−1) freedoms for the moving links, subtract the constraints each joint imposes, and count.

The first experiment applies it to twenty-two mechanisms and checks the answer against what each one actually does.

It is right 13 times out of 22, 59.1 per cent. The failures are not scattered. On the open chains — the ones where the joint count is one less than the link count — it is right 4 times out of 4, which is to say always. On closed loops it is right 9 times out of 18, which is to say half the time. The formula is not a formula about mechanisms. It is a formula about chains, and it happens to be exact when there are no loops.

Three ways to be wrong

The failures sort into three kinds and it is worth keeping them apart.

Idle freedoms. A Stewart platform built with spherical joints at both ends of every strut scores twelve when the formula is applied and delivers six. The other six are each strut spinning about its own axis, which is a real freedom of a real part that no load and no command ever reaches. The formula is right; the question was badly posed. Replace the lower spherical joints with universal joints and the arithmetic and the machine agree at six.

The wrong λ. A planar three-legged parallel mechanism scores three when counted as planar and minus three when counted as spatial. Both counts are mechanically meaningless as stated; what has happened is that the mechanism's links all lie in parallel planes, so a third of the constraints each joint nominally imposes are imposing something already imposed. This is the easy case of the third failure, dressed up.

Overconstraint. Six of the twenty-two are mechanisms that the formula says cannot move. A Sarrus linkage, published in 1853 as a way of getting a straight line without a sliding pair, scores zero and has one freedom.24 A Bennett linkage scores minus two and has one freedom.25, 26 A Goldberg five-bar scores minus one and has one.27 A Bricard or Schatz six-bar scores zero and has one.28, 29 Across the six, the shortfall averages 2.67 freedoms, and the shortfall is exactly the number of constraints that are not independent of the others.

The Bennett linkage is the sharpest case and worth dwelling on. Four revolute joints in a spatial loop should be rigid, and are, for almost every choice of link lengths and twist angles. For one particular family of choices — opposite links equal, and the ratio of each link's length to the sine of its twist angle the same for both pairs — the loop moves. Its mobility is a property of its dimensions, not of its topology, and no amount of counting links and joints can see it.30 This is why the serious treatments of mobility do not count at all; they compute the rank of a screw system, or work in the Lie group of displacements, and arrive at the answer the mechanism actually has.31, 32, 33, 10, 34, 35

Why overconstraint is worth having anyway

Exact straight-line generation is the oldest of these problems and the best documented: Peaucellier's inversor was the first exact solution, and Kempe's lecture remains the readable account of why it was hard.36, 37

An overconstrained mechanism is one whose constraints duplicate each other. That sounds like a defect and is often a feature, because duplicated constraints are load paths in parallel, and a load path in parallel is exactly what raises a machine's stiffness without raising its actuator count. The parallelogram loop at the core of every delta robot is overconstrained when counted spatially, and the reason the delta is fast is that those redundant constraints let three struts hold the platform's orientation while three motors move its position.38, 39

The price is that the mechanism now relies on dimensions rather than on topology. A Bennett linkage made to ordinary tolerances does not move at all. Every overconstrained mechanism trades manufacturing precision for stiffness, and the trade is invisible in the drawing.

Constraints imposed from outside the machine

One plate in this family exists for a reason with nothing to do with mechanism theory. A remote centre of motion linkage produces rotations about a point no part of the mechanism occupies, so that a surgical instrument can pivot about the opening it entered through without loading the tissue at the edge.40, 41 The constraint being satisfied is a boundary condition outside the machine altogether, and the type synthesis of linkages that satisfy it is a small literature of its own.42

05 — SERIAL

Serial manipulators

An open chain is the obvious way to build a machine that reaches: bolt a joint to the frame, a link to the joint, another joint to the link, and stop when you have enough freedoms. Every industrial arm in the world descends from Devol's transfer patent and Engelberger's Unimate,43, 44 and the vocabulary for describing one — a chain of frames related by four parameters per link — descends from Denavit and Hartenberg.45, 46 Scheinman's Stanford arm, an early all-electric design with a prismatic third axis, is where much of the analysis was first worked out on real hardware.47, 48, 49

The choice of which joints, in which order, is not a detail. It decides the shape of the workspace, the form of the inverse kinematics, and the answer to the question this article is about.

The Cartesian machine buys support and pays in floor

Three prismatic axes give three translations, and the tool's orientation is held by the portal frame and its guideways: rung five in all three rotations, the highest held set in the whole census. Nothing else comes close. The price appears when you measure how much of the space the machine occupies it can actually reach.

The fourth experiment builds five three-freedom positioners of declared geometry, counts their reachable volume by voxel occupancy, and divides by the axis-aligned box that contains every member at every admissible configuration — the box you have to fence.50 The gantry reaches 26.48 per cent of its own envelope. The articulated arm reaches 54.88 per cent. The machine with the highest held rung in the census is near the bottom of the chart and the machine with nothing held structurally is at the top, which is the trade in a single picture, and which is why the articulated arm won the factory.51

SCARA, and a limitation of the gauge

Makino's selective compliance assembly robot arm, developed at the University of Yamanashi from 1978 through an industry consortium and into production by 1981, is the sharpest piece of architectural reasoning in the field.52, 53 Its two main revolute axes are vertical. A vertical force on the tool therefore produces no moment about either of them, so it never reaches those gear trains at all; it goes through the links and into the shoulder bearings. A horizontal force produces a large moment about both, at the full moment arm of the extended arm, and goes straight into the gearboxes. The machine is stiff in the direction a peg is pushed and compliant in the directions a peg has to wiggle to find its hole.

On the hold card this does not show. Both directions come out on rung two, because the quill carrying the vertical stroke is itself a screw, and the ladder records the kind of support and not its magnitude. This is the gauge failing to see something real, and it is worth saying plainly rather than patching the gauge until it agrees. What the ladder captures is what is in the load path; what it misses is that the same kind of element, at a moment arm of zero rather than half a metre, is a different component in every way that matters.

The articulated arm holds nothing

A six-revolute arm has all six lanes amber. There are no held lanes on its card at all. Every direction in which you might push its tool is resisted by a gear train, and when the power fails the only thing between the payload and the floor is a set of brakes. It is also why an industrial arm's repeatability and its absolute accuracy differ by an order of magnitude or more: repeatability is a property of the encoders, and accuracy is a property of everything between them and the tool.54, 55, 56, 57 Two other plates share this property — the redundant seven-axis arm, which is the same thing with one more compliance in series, and the cable robot, for a different reason — and they are the only ones.

A seventh joint changes none of this. Redundancy buys the ability to reach around an obstacle, to stay away from joint limits, and to choose a posture that improves the conditioning of the Jacobian, and all of that is real.58, 59, 60 On this gauge it also adds one more compliance in series and no support whatever, which is why the redundant plate carries the highest path count in the census.

This is not a criticism. It is the reason the architecture exists. Nothing held structurally means nothing in the way, and nothing in the way is what buys the reach-to-envelope ratio on the chart above, and the reach-to-envelope ratio is what sells robots.

The wrist, and a decision with two faces

Three revolute axes meeting at a point give the tool three rotations about that point and give the analyst something much more valuable: the inverse kinematics decouples. The position of the wrist centre depends only on the first three joints, the orientation only on the last three, and the whole problem falls apart into two problems of three unknowns each with a closed-form solution.61, 62 Without a decoupling condition of this kind the general six-revolute inverse problem is a polynomial of degree sixteen and has no closed form at all.63, 64

The seventh experiment builds such an arm from screw axes and sweeps the determinant of its Jacobian.

Over twelve random settings of the other five joints and six values of the middle wrist joint, the ratio of the determinant's magnitude to the sine of that joint's angle varies by at most 1.664e-14 — machine precision. The joint enters the determinant as a factor entirely of its own. Set it to zero and the first and third wrist axes coincide, the arm loses a rotational freedom, and no command to the other five joints recovers it. On a grid of 13,824 poses, 15.23 per cent sit within two per cent of the largest determinant found, and 54.7 per cent of those are attributable to the wrist.

The decoupling and the singularity are the same design decision seen from two sides. You make three axes intersect so that the algebra separates; the algebra separates because a factor came out; the factor that came out vanishes somewhere; where it vanishes the machine is lame. There is no version of this arm that has the closed form and not the surface.

06 — PARALLEL

Parallel mechanisms and parallel robots

Close the chain and everything changes at once. The actuators can sit on the ground instead of being carried; the load divides among several paths instead of travelling down one; the forward kinematics becomes hard and the inverse kinematics becomes easy, which is the reverse of the serial case; and the singularities move from the edge of the workspace into the middle of it.

The two inventions

The six-strut platform is usually called a Stewart platform after a 1965 paper proposing one as a flight simulator motion base.65 The machine in general use is not the one in that paper: it is Gough's tyre-testing rig, operational at Dunlop from 1954 and described to the FISITA congress in 1962, which is why the careful literature says Gough–Stewart or Gough–Whitehall.66, 67 Klaus Cappel arrived at the same architecture independently around the same time. Its forward kinematics — given six strut lengths, where is the platform? — has up to forty solutions in the complex field, a result that took until the 1990s to settle.68, 69, 70, 71, 72

The delta is a later and more specific idea. Reymond Clavel's insight, filed as WO 87/03528 in 1987 and granted as US 4,976,582 in 1990, was to use three parallelograms to remove all three rotations from a moving platform, leaving three pure translations and allowing all three motors to remain on the frame.73, 74, 75, 38, 76, 77 The moving mass is three light rods and a small plate, and the accelerations follow from that.

What the closed chain actually buys

The second experiment puts a two-link serial arm and a symmetric five-bar side by side with the same links, the same two actuators and the same joint stiffness, and maps the stiffness in the weakest direction across every point both can reach.

Across 9,126 shared points the five-bar's median is 67,573 newtons per metre against the serial arm's 40,320, a ratio of 1.455. But the minima tell a better story than the medians: the serial arm's floor over the whole region is 17,341 newtons per metre and the five-bar's is 11. At 10.90 per cent of points the closed chain is the softer of the two. A parallel machine is stiffer almost everywhere and catastrophically soft on a set it carries around inside its own workspace.

The stiffness of a closed chain is a mature subject with a standard apparatus: a stiffness map derived from the Jacobian and the actuator stiffnesses, refined by matrix structural analysis when the links themselves matter.78, 79, 80, 81 It is the analysis that decides whether a robot can cut metal, and the answer is usually that it cannot, because an articulated arm's static stiffness at the tool sits one to two orders of magnitude below a machine tool's.82, 83 The parallel kinematic machine tool exists to close that gap, and the hybrid tripod-plus-wrist layouts in commercial use are the shape the compromise took.84

Errors: one path or many

The fifth experiment gives every actuator the same relative error — one part in ten thousand of its own full travel — and asks what arrives at the tool.

In an open chain of equal revolutes holding total reach at one metre, the amplification grows from 1.1180 to 1.6903 as the joint count goes from two to seven: 51.2 per cent worse for adding freedoms that do not extend the reach at all. In the six-strut platform the six errors travel six paths and divide: the amplification is 1.4833, against the square root of six that six identical errors in series would give, and the tool error comes out at 44.50 micrometres against the serial six-revolute arm's 999.0.

That ratio of 22.4 deserves an honest footnote, because it rests on what "full travel" means for a revolute. A strut's stroke here is three hundred millimetres; a revolute's range is taken as a whole turn. Halve that assumption and the ratio halves. The point survives anyway, and it is arithmetic rather than engineering: an encoder on a rotary joint has to resolve a whole revolution to the same fractional precision that a linear scale resolves three hundred millimetres, and the two jobs are not equally hard.

Cables, and constraints that only pull

A cable-driven parallel robot replaces the struts with winches and the building becomes the frame.21, 85 Its path count is the lowest in the census. Its problem is that a cable holds in tension and holds nothing in compression, so the platform is controllable only where a set of strictly positive tensions exists that produces the required wrench. That region — the wrench-feasible workspace — is a genuinely different object from a reachable workspace, and computing it is the central problem of the field.20, 86

Two cautionary plates

The spherical parallel wrist does the serial wrist's job with three curved links whose axes all pass through one point, at a third of the path count and a small fraction of the moving mass.87, 88 The 3-UPU translational mechanism is the field's standing warning: a design the mobility analysis says gives three pure translations, and which in one assembly turned out to gain an uncontrollable rotation near its home pose.89, 90, 91 The dimensions were right and the topology was right; what was missing was a check that the constraint system keeps its rank throughout the workspace rather than merely at the pose where it was analysed.

07 — SINGULAR

The two kinds of singularity

A mechanism is singular when its Jacobian loses rank, and the sentence is short enough to hide that two quite different things are being described. The distinction is Gosselin and Angeles's and it is the most useful single idea in parallel kinematics.92, 93, 94

A type 1 or serial singularity is a loss of motion: the mechanism cannot move the tool in some direction. It happens where a chain straightens or folds, which is to say at the boundary of the region the chain can reach. You can decline to go there.

A type 2 or parallel singularity is a loss of constraint: the mechanism cannot resist a force in some direction, and the platform gains an instantaneous freedom that no actuator can lock. Nothing requires this to happen at a boundary, and in general it does not.

The third experiment sweeps the same five-bar as before, but through each of its four assembly modes in turn, and counts the interior grid points where the condition number exceeds a hundred. A point is interior when all four of its neighbours are reachable too.

mechanismreachable points near singularof which interior
2R, elbow up47,7090.025%0.000%
2R, elbow down47,7090.025%0.000%
five-bar up/down42,6790.084%0.000%
five-bar up/up42,6791.931%1.884%
five-bar down/up42,6790.951%0.959%
five-bar down/down42,6791.931%1.884%

The open chain has no interior singularity in either of its two configurations: not a small number, zero. The five-bar has interior singularities in 3 of its 4 assembly modes, running to 1.884 per cent of interior points. The dimensions never changed. The link lengths are identical in all six cases. What changed was which way the elbows were put together when the machine was assembled, and that alone decided whether there is a surface in the middle of the working volume on which the machine cannot hold the tool against a load.

This is the reason working modes and assembly modes are first-class objects in the parallel-robot literature rather than an afterthought, and why the useful workspace of a parallel machine is always some singularity-free cell carved out of the reachable one.95, 96, 97, 98 A serial machine's designer draws the workspace and then subtracts the edges. A parallel machine's designer finds the singular variety first and then asks what is left.

The practical form of the difference: a serial singularity announces itself as a commanded motion that will not happen, which a controller can detect and refuse. A parallel singularity announces itself as a machine that was holding its position and is now not, under a load that has not changed. The second is worse in every respect, including the respect that matters for safety.99

08 — BRAKE

When a transmission becomes a brake

Nineteen of the forty plates are complete machines. On 17 of them the lowest-rung moved direction is held by a transmission. The ladder's second rung is where robots live, so it is worth asking precisely what that rung promises and what it costs, and the answer is exact rather than approximate.

Take the cleanest case, a power screw, where the whole geometry is one angle. The classical relations give the torque to raise a load and the torque to lower it; the mechanism is self-locking when the lowering torque comes out positive, meaning you would have to push to let the load down.100, 101

For a square thread of twenty millimetres mean diameter and a friction coefficient of one tenth, the sixth experiment finds the boundary by bisection at a lead of 6.2832 millimetres, a lead angle of 5.7106 degrees. At that boundary the tangent of the lead angle equals the friction coefficient exactly, as the algebra predicts, and the forward efficiency is 0.4950.

That number is not a coincidence and it does not depend on the diameter. At the self-locking boundary the efficiency of a square-threaded screw is (1 − tan²λ)/2, which approaches one half from below as the lead angle goes to zero and never reaches it. A transmission that holds its load without power is one that wastes more than half of what you put into it. The same relation appears in the general form: a simple machine's reverse efficiency is 2 − 1/η, which is zero exactly at η = 0.5.

The sensitivity is worth noting too. Across friction coefficients from 0.05 to 0.20 — a range that a change of lubricant covers — the boundary lead moves by a factor of 4.00. Self-locking is therefore specified with a margin and is never relied on as a safety function by itself, which is why robot joints carry brakes.99

The inertia the gearbox hands back

The second half of the experiment tabulates representative drivetrains with declared generic efficiencies and asks two questions of each: can it be back- driven, and what does its rotor look like from the joint?

drivetrainratio η forwardη reverse N²Jm, kg·m² as a fraction of the link
direct drive11.001.0000.00010.000
toothed belt, 3:130.960.9580.00050.000
planetary, 10:1100.940.9360.00500.005
ball screw + arm200.900.8890.02000.020
cycloidal, 59:1590.850.8240.17410.174
harmonic drive, 100:11000.780.7180.50000.500
harmonic drive, 160:11600.750.6671.28001.280
acme lead screw400.35-0.8570.08000.080
worm, 40:1400.45-0.2220.08000.080

Two of the nine cannot be back-driven at all: their reverse efficiency is negative, which is what self-locking looks like in this column. Those two hold their load with the power off and give nothing back. At the other end, the direct drive gives everything back and holds nothing.

Between them sits the harmonic drive, which is why it is in almost every industrial arm.102, 103, 104 At a hundred to one its reverse efficiency is 0.718, comfortably back-drivable on paper. But its rotor, multiplied by the square of the ratio, presents 0.50 kilogram metres squared at the joint — half of the link's own inertia in this model. At a hundred and sixty to one it presents 1.28, more than the link. A joint like that is back-drivable in the steady state and not in a collision, which is a distinction the ladder does not draw and a person walking past the machine very much does.105, 106

The crossing point is clean: reflected rotor inertia equals link inertia at a ratio of the square root of their ratio, here N = 141.4. Above it the motor is the heaviest thing in the joint, seen from outside.

This is the whole of the transparency problem, and every answer to it is a choice about which rung to stand on. Put a spring in the path and you drop to rung one on purpose, and get force sensing for nothing.107, 108 Take the gearbox out and you drop to rung one by omission, and get a limb that folds when the power fails.109 Add variable stiffness and you buy the ability to move between rungs at runtime, at the cost of another actuator.110, 111

09 — HUMANOID

Humanoid and legged mechanisms

A legged machine has a requirement no arm has: it must survive contact it did not plan. An arm that hits something can stop. A leg that hits the ground is doing its job, several times a second, and the impulse arrives before any control loop can respond to it.112, 113, 114 This turns the choice of rung from a preference into the central design decision.

Three answers are in current use and the census carries all three.

Rung two, with a brake. A geared joint holds the limb up without power and presents a large reflected inertia to the ground. The first generation of walking humanoids was built this way, and the control problem was posed as trajectory tracking with a stability criterion, because the hardware offered nothing else.115, 116, 117

Rung one, on purpose. A series-elastic actuator puts a calibrated spring between the gearbox and the load. The spring is soft, so the joint is soft, which sounds like a loss until you notice that measuring the spring's deflection gives you joint torque for free and at high bandwidth.107, 108 It is the only plate in the census where a designer deliberately lowered a rung, and the thing bought is a sense of touch distributed through the whole limb. The cost is an upper bound on bandwidth set by the spring's own resonance.

Rung one, by omission. A quasi-direct-drive leg uses a large-diameter motor and a gear ratio small enough that the reflected inertia stays below the limb's own.109, 118 The joint is transparent: an impact at the foot is felt at the rotor, and the rotor can push back within a millisecond. This is why the current generation of legged machines can run on ground they have not surveyed.119, 120 What they cannot do is stand still with the power off, and the energetic accounting of that choice — what a legged machine spends, and on what — is now a subject in its own right.121

Moving the mass off the end of the limb

The other structural move that recurs in legged design is closing the chain locally. A two-actuator parallel ankle puts both motors at the top of the shank and drives the foot through struts,122 so the mass that the leg has to swing is a pair of light rods rather than a pair of motors. The plate's path count is 0.500, half of a serial equivalent, and its held directions are carried by struts rather than by bending. The cost is the usual one: the two strut lines become parallel at the limit of roll, and the mechanism has a type 2 singularity inside a range of motion it genuinely needs.

Hands: when the mechanism decides

A human hand has more than twenty joints. Actuating twenty joints in a robot hand is possible and has been done, at great cost in volume, mass and tendon routing.123, 124 The alternative is underactuation: give the finger fewer inputs than joints and let the mechanism distribute the motion according to what it touches.125, 126, 127, 128, 129

The ninth experiment takes the simplest case — two phalanges, one tendon, two pulleys — and computes the contact forces. The distal force is always positive. The proximal force can go negative, at which point the finger is levering the object out of its own grasp. The condition for a stable grasp works out to a comparison between the pulley ratio and a quantity built from the distal contact position and the joint angle:

f1 > 0  ⇔  r1/r2 > (l1 cosθ2 + k2) / k2

The proximal contact position k1 does not appear. Two hundred combinations of the other variables were checked across twenty values of k1 each, and the sign never changed once: where an object touches the proximal phalanx has no bearing whatever on whether the hand keeps hold of it. At a pulley ratio of one, 0.00 per cent of contact geometries are stable. At three, 53.78 per cent. Restricting the distal contact to the outer three quarters of the phalanx, where an object of any real size actually touches, a ratio of 3.37 covers three quarters of the range and 4.51 covers nine tenths.

Those are machined dimensions. Once the pulleys are cut, the set of objects the hand can hold is fixed, and no controller reaches it — there is one command travelling down one tendon, and the mechanism decides the rest. That is precisely what underactuation buys, and precisely what it costs.

10 — SOFT

Soft robotics

Soft robotics is usually introduced as the absence of the things the rest of this article is about: no joints, no links, no discrete freedoms.130, 131, 132, 133 That framing is wrong in a way that the hold cards make visible. A silicone arm bending under a tendon is not unsupported. The material is holding the shape, in bending, exactly as a flexure hinge does. Softness is not an absence of structure. It is a structure with a different modulus.

The eighth experiment makes the size of the difference concrete. Three cantilevers of the same length and the same outside diameter: an aluminium tube, a solid glass-fibre rod, a solid cast silicone rod. The bending stiffness of the aluminium tube exceeds the silicone's by a factor of 23,729.

That is what has been given away, and the thing bought with it is substantial: a machine that can strike an obstacle, or a person, and neither break nor injure, without a single sensor being involved in the outcome.106, 111 The compliance is the safety mechanism. For a whole class of tasks — handling produce, working inside a body, reaching into a space whose shape is not known — that trade is obviously correct.

What the model gives up

The standard kinematic model for a continuum segment assumes it bends in a circular arc of constant curvature, which reduces an infinite-dimensional shape to two or three numbers and makes everything downstream tractable.134 The second half of the experiment asks what that assumption costs, by solving the same silicone segment as a large-deflection elastica under nothing but its own weight and then fitting the best single circle to the result.

The fit is out by 13.21 millimetres at the tip, which is 4.40 per cent of the segment's own length, at zero applied load. The reason is a boundary condition rather than a numerical detail: a free end carries no moment, so the curvature there must be zero, while at the root it is 4.610 per metre. No loaded segment of this kind is a circular arc, and no refinement of the manufacturing will make it one. Adding a tip load makes it worse, reaching 15.30 millimetres at 0.40 newtons.

This is not an argument against the model, which remains the right first thing to use. It is an argument about where the error lives. The constant- curvature model is not wrong about the shape; it is wrong about the shape's dependence on load, and a mechanism with no structural hold on any direction is one whose shape depends on load in every direction at once. The serious modelling work in the field — Cosserat rods, finite-element formulations, learned residuals — is all in one way or another an attempt to buy that dependence back.135, 136, 137

Three ways out

Three plates in this family show what the field does about it. The pneumatic bending actuator adds a strain-limiting layer: one inextensible face that turns an isotropic balloon into something that bends in a chosen plane, which is a single structural direction bought cheaply.138, 139, 140 Granular jamming does something stranger: it delivers no motion at all, and what it delivers instead is a switch between a fluid and a solid on one vacuum line — a mechanism whose output is a change of rung.141 The eversion robot changes the question by growing, so that its envelope is not fixed when it is built, and its tip does not slide against anything it passes.142, 143 Artificial muscles of various chemistries remain, on this gauge, tendon elements with actuators in them, with the same unilateral problem: they pull, and something else has to push.144, 145
