==============================================================================
E3  TWO KINDS OF SINGULARITY, AND WHERE THEY LIVE
==============================================================================
A serial chain loses rank when it straightens, and the straightened
poses are the boundary of its own workspace: you can decline to go
there.  A closed chain loses rank when its constraint directions
become dependent, and nothing says that has to happen at an edge.
Same links and same two actuators as E2.  A point counts as INTERIOR
when all four of its neighbours on the grid are reachable too.

-- the open chain
2R, elbow up           reachable  47709   well-conditioned  97.34%   near-singular 0.025%   INTERIOR near-singular 0.000%
2R, elbow down         reachable  47709   well-conditioned  97.34%   near-singular 0.025%   INTERIOR near-singular 0.000%

-- the closed chain, one working mode at a time
five-bar up/down       reachable  42679   well-conditioned  98.13%   near-singular 0.084%   INTERIOR near-singular 0.000%
five-bar up/up         reachable  42679   well-conditioned  81.22%   near-singular 1.931%   INTERIOR near-singular 1.884%
five-bar down/up       reachable  42679   well-conditioned  90.35%   near-singular 0.951%   INTERIOR near-singular 0.959%
five-bar down/down     reachable  42679   well-conditioned  81.22%   near-singular 1.931%   INTERIOR near-singular 1.884%

-- what the comparison shows
worst interior near-singular fraction, open chain   : 0.0000%
closed-chain working modes with interior singularities: 3 of 4
   five-bar up/down       0.000%
   five-bar up/up         1.884%
   five-bar down/up       0.959%
   five-bar down/down     1.884%
The dimensions never changed.  The mode in which the mechanism was
assembled decided whether there is a surface in the middle of the
workspace on which the machine cannot resist a force.  The open
chain has no such surface in any configuration, because its
singularities are the places it cannot reach in the first place.

==============================================================================
E5  DO ACTUATOR ERRORS ADD UP OR AVERAGE OUT?
==============================================================================
Every actuator is given the same RELATIVE error: epsilon of its own
full travel, independent, zero mean.  The question is what arrives
at the tool.  RMS tool position error = eps_i-weighted Frobenius
norm of the map from actuator error to tool displacement.

-- serial chain: n equal revolute joints, total reach 1.000 m, straight
   n    amp (m/rad)     trav (rad)     err (um)
   2         1.1180         6.2832      702.481
   3         1.2472         6.2832      783.651
   4         1.3693         6.2832      860.361
   5         1.4832         6.2832      931.947
   6         1.5899         6.2832      998.963
   7         1.6903         6.2832     1062.052
amplification from 2 joints to 7 joints: 1.118 -> 1.690  (+51.2%)

-- Stewart-Gough platform, six struts, home pose
strut lengths at home : 0.7399, 0.7399, 0.7399, 0.7399, 0.7399, 0.7399 m
position amplification (dimensionless) : 1.4833
orientation amplification (1/m)        : 4.8999
strut stroke 0.30 m, eps 1e-04  ->  RMS tool error 44.499 um
if the six struts were instead stacked in series, six independent
errors would add along one path and the amplification would be
sqrt(6) = 2.4495 against the parallel machine's 1.4833  (1.65x better)
pairing each platform point to the base point beneath it instead
gives |det| = 1.6e-50 at the same home pose, which is zero to machine
precision: the rotationally symmetric platform is singular where it
stands, and no controller reaches a rank the mechanism does not have.

-- six-revolute serial arm, reach 1.000 m
amplification 1.5899 m/rad, full travel 2*pi rad -> 998.963 um
ratio serial-6R error / Stewart error : 22.45x

the comparison rests on what 'full travel' means for a revolute,
so here it is at three assumptions:
  revolute travel a whole turn    998.963 um   ratio to Stewart  22.45x
  revolute travel half a turn     499.481 um   ratio to Stewart  11.22x
  revolute travel a quarter turn  249.741 um   ratio to Stewart   5.61x
even at a quarter turn the serial chain is the worse of the two,
and the reason is arithmetic rather than engineering: an encoder on
a revolute has to resolve its whole range to the same fraction that
a linear scale resolves a stroke of three hundred millimetres.

==============================================================================
E6  WHEN A TRANSMISSION BECOMES A BRAKE
==============================================================================
A drivetrain holds a direction without power only when it refuses to
run backwards.  For a simple machine the reverse efficiency is
eta_back = 2 - 1/eta_fwd, which is zero at eta_fwd = 0.50 exactly.

-- square-thread power screw, mean diameter 20 mm, mu = 0.10
 lead mm lambda deg      eta fwd  T_lower N.m     locks?
   1.000      0.912       0.1371       0.8395        yes
   2.000      1.823       0.2407       0.6795        yes
   3.000      2.734       0.3216       0.5201        yes
   4.000      3.643       0.3865       0.3611        yes
   5.000      4.550       0.4396       0.2026        yes
   6.283      5.710       0.4950       0.0000        yes
   8.000      7.256       0.5530      -0.2698         no
  10.000      9.043       0.6044      -0.5823         no
  14.000     12.561       0.6748      -1.2014         no
  20.000     17.657       0.7367      -2.1158         no

self-locking boundary at lead 6.2832 mm, lead angle 5.7106 deg
efficiency AT the boundary                   : 0.4950
tan(lambda) at the boundary                  : 0.1000 (= mu, as predicted)
closed form for the boundary efficiency, (1 - tan^2 lambda)/2 : 0.4950
so a self-locking screw can never exceed 50% efficiency, and the
holding you get for free is paid for twice over in the forward
direction.  There is no configuration that buys both.

-- how much of the design sits on the friction coefficient
      mu boundary lead mm boundary lambda
   0.050         3.1416         2.8624
   0.080         5.0265         4.5739
   0.100         6.2832         5.7106
   0.120         7.5398         6.8428
   0.150         9.4248         8.5308
   0.200        12.5664        11.3099
the boundary lead moves 4.00x across a friction range that a change
of lubricant covers, which is why self-locking is specified with a
margin and never relied on as a safety function on its own.

link's own inertia: 2 of 9
  harmonic drive, 100:1, harmonic drive, 160:1
Nothing in this table is both transparent and stiff: the two
columns move in opposite directions, and that is the whole reason
a robot's moved directions sit low on the support ladder.

==============================================================================
E7  DOES ONE JOINT OWN A WHOLE SINGULAR SURFACE?
==============================================================================
Six-revolute arm, spherical wrist, upper arm 0.50 m, forearm 0.50 m.
The Jacobian mixes metres and radians, so rotational rows are scaled
by a characteristic length Lc = 1.000 m; this changes the numerical
value of the determinant but not where it vanishes.

-- is det J separable in t5?
configurations tested      : 12
t5 values per configuration: 6
max relative deviation of |det J| / |sin t5| over t5 : 1.664e-14
mean relative deviation                              : 1.877e-15
The ratio is constant to machine precision, so t5 enters the
determinant as a factor on its own: the wrist singularity is a
property of one joint and survives every choice of the other five.

-- how much of joint space is near singular
grid 24^3 over (t2, t3, t5) at fixed t1, t4, t6 : 13824 poses
|det J| below 2% of its maximum on the grid  : 2106 (15.23%)
  attributable to the wrist     :  1152 (54.70% of the near-singular set)
  attributable to the elbow     :   528 (25.07% of the near-singular set)
  attributable to the shoulder  :   296 (14.06% of the near-singular set)
  attributable to the other     :   130 (6.17% of the near-singular set)
Only one of these three is a defect of the mechanism rather than of
the pose: the wrist surface exists wherever three axes are made to
intersect, which is the very property that gives the arm a closed-
form inverse solution.  The decoupling and the singularity are the
same design decision seen from two sides.

E8  WHAT A SOFT ARM GIVES UP
==============================================================================

-- bending stiffness of three cantilevers of the same length and girth
length 0.30 m, outside diameter 40 mm; tip load 0.5 N.
member                           E (Pa)      EI (N.m2)    tip defl mm
aluminium tube 2 mm wall      6.900e+10      2981.8866         0.0015
glass-fibre rod, solid        4.000e+10      5026.5482         0.0009
cast silicone, solid          1.000e+06         0.1257        35.8099

the small-deflection formula is quoted for all three so that the
comparison is like for like; at 0.5 N the silicone is already far
outside its range, and the large-deflection solver below is what
that member's real shape comes from.
bending stiffness ratio, aluminium tube to silicone : 23729 : 1
Four and a half orders of magnitude of stiffness given away, in
exchange for a machine that can hit something and not break it.

-- does constant curvature survive the segment's own weight?
silicone segment: EI = 0.1257 N.m2, self weight 13.560 N/m over 0.30 m
tip load  0.00 N : best circle kappa  -2.543 1/m; true kappa  -4.610 at the root and  -0.000 at the tip; RMS  5.557 mm, tip error 13.209 mm
tip load  0.05 N : best circle kappa  -2.612 1/m; true kappa  -4.709 at the root and  -0.000 at the tip; RMS  5.660 mm, tip error 13.475 mm
tip load  0.10 N : best circle kappa  -2.680 1/m; true kappa  -4.807 at the root and  -0.001 at the tip; RMS  5.762 mm, tip error 13.740 mm
tip load  0.20 N : best circle kappa  -2.813 1/m; true kappa  -4.999 at the root and  -0.001 at the tip; RMS  5.965 mm, tip error 14.265 mm
tip load  0.40 N : best circle kappa  -3.067 1/m; true kappa  -5.372 at the root and  -0.002 at the tip; RMS  6.366 mm, tip error 15.301 mm

A free end carries no moment, so the curvature there has to vanish:
0.0001 1/m at the tip, zero to the discretisation, against 4.610 1/m
at the root.  No loaded segment of this kind is a circular arc, and
the error that assumption makes is not a small one.
Under self weight alone the best single circle is out by 13.21 mm at
the tip, which is 4.40% of the segment's own length.
Worst case in this sweep: tip load 0.40 N, tip error 15.30 mm (5.10% of length).
The model is not wrong about the shape; it is wrong about the
shape's dependence on load, which is exactly what a mechanism with
no structural hold on any direction cannot avoid.

E9  WHAT DECIDES WHETHER AN UNDERACTUATED GRASP HOLDS
==============================================================================
Two phalanges (60 mm, 40 mm), one tendon, pulley ratio R = r1/r2.
Contact at k1 along the proximal phalanx and k2 along the distal.
The distal force is always positive; the proximal force can go
negative, at which point the object is levered out of the hand.
R =  1.0 : stable contacts       0 of   54000  (  0.00%), mean f1/f2  0.000
R =  1.5 : stable contacts    7260 of   54000  ( 13.44%), mean f1/f2  0.613
R =  2.0 : stable contacts   13140 of   54000  ( 24.33%), mean f1/f2  1.119
R =  2.5 : stable contacts   20580 of   54000  ( 38.11%), mean f1/f2  1.550
R =  3.0 : stable contacts   29040 of   54000  ( 53.78%), mean f1/f2  2.029
R =  4.0 : stable contacts   37440 of   54000  ( 69.33%), mean f1/f2  3.440
R =  6.0 : stable contacts   44280 of   54000  ( 82.00%), mean f1/f2  6.491

-- what the stability condition does and does not depend on
f1 > 0  <=>  R > (l1 cos th2 + k2) / k2 .
k1 does not appear.  Where the object touches the PROXIMAL phalanx
has no bearing at all on whether the finger keeps hold of it.
checked 200 (k2, theta2) pairs across 20 values of k1 each: 0 showed
any dependence of the sign on k1.
pulley ratio needed for 50% of contact pairs to be stable: 2.85
pulley ratio needed for 75% of contact pairs to be stable: 4.66
pulley ratio needed for 90% of contact pairs to be stable: 9.80
pulley ratio needed for 99% of contact pairs to be stable: 48.88

-- the same question with contacts kept off the distal joint
as k2 goes to zero the condition cannot be met at any ratio, so
restrict the distal contact to the outer three quarters of the
phalanx, which is where an object of any size actually touches:
  ratio for 50% of contacts to be stable: 2.57
  ratio for 75% of contacts to be stable: 3.37
  ratio for 90% of contacts to be stable: 4.51
  ratio for 99% of contacts to be stable: 6.48
A ratio of about 3.4 covers three quarters of the range, and the
remaining quarter is not reachable by any ratio a hand can carry.
The number is a machined dimension.  Once the pulleys are cut, the
set of objects the hand can hold is fixed, and no controller reaches
it: the tendon carries one command and the mechanism decides the
rest.  That is what underactuation buys and what it costs.

==============================================================================
12 — LEDGER

The ledger

Forty mechanisms, each on its two scalars and its path count.

The distributions are lopsided in the direction the opening question predicted, and by a measurable amount. Across every plate that holds anything, the mean held rung is 3.5833. Across every plate that moves anything, the mean moved rung is 1.5128. The gap is 2.0705 rungs, and it is the whole subject in one number: mechanisms are good at resisting what they are not for.

Restrict attention to the nineteen complete machines — the serial manipulators, the parallel mechanisms and the legged plates — and the moved-rung column nearly collapses. 17 of the 19 sit on rung two. The two exceptions are the series-elastic actuator and the quasi-direct-drive leg, which are on rung one, and are on rung one deliberately. Not one complete machine in this census holds a direction it moves with structure.

So D, which the opening question was really asking about, turns out to be nearly constant. The quantity that varies is nu. Across the same nineteen machines it runs from 0.1250 to 7.0000, a spread of 56.0x or 1.748 decades. The serial family averages 3.1429; the parallel family averages 0.4375; the ratio is 7.18x. Nothing on the support ladder sees any of that.

It would be too neat to claim that this ratio is the stiffness ratio or the error ratio, and it is not. nu is a count of topology; the second experiment measured a median stiffness ratio of 1.455 across a shared planar workspace, and the fifth measured an error ratio of 22.4x between a six-revolute arm and a six-strut platform. The three numbers disagree because they are measuring different consequences of the same arrangement, and because nu deliberately ignores how the load actually divides. What they agree on is direction and order of magnitude: the quantity that separates one complete machine from another is how many elements stand in the load path and how many paths share it, and every one of the three ways of asking gives the closed chain the advantage.

Which description separates mechanisms

A useful test of any classification is how many pairs of items it tells apart. Over the 780 pairs in a forty-item census:

descriptionpairs separated
family alone82.95%
D alone69.74%
H alone77.05%
nu bucket alone59.23%
D x H92.69%
D x nu bucket89.62%
D x H x nu bucket96.54%
the full six-lane card98.59%

Family alone does respectably, which is expected, since the families were chosen by someone who already knew the answer. D alone does worst of the single descriptors, which is the collapse above showing up as an information measure. D and H together reach 92.69 per cent; adding the path count reaches 96.54 per cent; and the full six-lane card, which is thirty-six bits of description rather than three numbers, reaches 98.59 per cent. The three-number summary recovers most of what the whole card knows, which is the case for using it.

The opening question asked what holds the direction you want to move. The honest answer, for anything that counts as a robot, is a motor and its gearbox, almost without exception, and the interesting question is therefore not which rung but how many. That is a less satisfying answer than the question promised, and it is the one the census gives.

13 — LIMITS

Limits and scope

What the gauge does not measure, stated plainly, because a gauge whose blind spots are hidden is worse than no gauge.

the ladder measures kind, not magnitude

This is the big one and it has been flagged twice already in the text. Rung three covers a steel flexure and a silicone backbone whose moduli differ by more than four orders of magnitude. Rung two covers a SCARA's shoulder gearbox at a half-metre moment arm and the same gearbox at no moment arm at all. Two lanes on the same rung can differ by any factor you like in newtons per metre. The ladder tells you what is in the load path and what will happen when the power goes; it does not tell you how far the tool moves under a kilogram.

the path count is a topology count

nu counts compliant elements in series and load paths in parallel. It does not weight them. Six struts sharing a load equally and six struts of which one carries nearly all of it have the same nu and very different behaviour, and the second case is exactly what happens near a type 2 singularity. The stiffness map in the sixth section is the corrective: it measures what nu only counts.

the cards are drawn at a nominal pose

A mechanism's load paths change as it moves. A telescoping boom's overlap shrinks as it extends; a five-bar's two legs stop sharing as the tool leaves the centre; an articulated arm's worst gearbox depends on where the payload is. Each card is drawn for the configuration in which the mechanism is normally described, and E2, E3 and E7 exist because that is not enough.

the census is a chosen sample

Forty mechanisms selected to span the field are not a random sample of anything, and the separation percentages in the ledger should be read as a property of this list rather than as an estimate about mechanisms in general. The families were chosen first and the scalars computed second.

what the lab models, and what it does not

All geometry is declared and generic. No manufacturer's kinematic data, product dimensions, control parameters or proprietary efficiency figures appear anywhere; the drivetrain efficiencies in the eighth section are round numbers chosen to sit in the middle of published ranges, and the conclusions drawn from them depend on the ordering rather than on the values. The lumped models are deliberately simple: joint stiffnesses are scalar and configuration- independent, links are rigid except where the experiment is about their bending, friction appears only in the screw analysis, and dynamics appear nowhere at all. Every one of those simplifications would matter for a design and none of them changes the structural point being made.

standards move

The safety references here are to the third editions of ISO 10218-1 and 10218-2, published in 2025, which absorb the collaborative-operation material formerly in ISO/TS 15066 and introduce the Class 1 and Class 2 robot distinction.99, 50, 146 ISO 9283, the performance test standard whose form the masthead of this article borrows, dates from 1998 and was reviewed and confirmed in 2021.54 ISO 8373:2021 remains the vocabulary of record, with a revision in progress.147 Anyone using this article as a route into the standards should check the current status rather than trusting this paragraph.

one more thing the article does not do

It says nothing about control. Every mechanism here is examined as a structure, at rest or moving quasi-statically. That is a real restriction: a great deal of what a modern robot can do is a property of its loops rather than its links, and impedance control in particular can make a stiff joint behave softly within the bandwidth of the loop.148, 149, 150, 151 What it cannot do is change the rung. When the power goes, what is left is the mechanism.
